title: Testing every journal entry with machine-learning anomaly scoring
problem: Journal-entry testing is a required fraud response, but rules filters on very large ledgers miss subtler patterns and flood teams with false positives.
approach: A tool scores every ledger entry and shows why items look unusual; auditors select from them. Users include BDO UK and KPMG.
Regulators saw automated tools in journal-entry testing in 88% of cases in 2024 (independent); all six US network firms reported them (self-reported).
The team follows up each high-risk item and stays alert to signs the tool is systematically flawed for the engagement.
who: Buzzacott, BDO UK, KPMG, EY, MindBridge

title: Idea: language-model anomaly detection with written explanations for journal entries
problem: This is an idea, not a deployment: rule-based journal-entry tests produce many false positives, and machine-learning scores do not explain themselves.
approach: Researchers prompt language models with each ledger record plus a classical anomaly score, asking for a yes/no flag and a plain-language explanation.
On a synthetic ledger, the best open model had 12 false positives against 942 for rules-based testing, with 2 missed anomalies (independent).
The auditor reviews each flagged entry with the model's explanation before treating it as an exception.

title: Evidence-linked triage of items flagged by whole-population tests
problem: Whole-population tests surface more items to follow up, and thin testing of outliers is among regulators' most common technology findings.
approach: MindBridge says its Augmented Assurance offering lets auditors drill into the entries, accounts or periods driving risk, using the system's explanations (vendor-published).
Its Agentic Risk Assessment, announced September 2026, is positioned for audit planning, not for following up flagged items.
The auditor investigates and documents the rationale for concluding on flagged and additional items.

title: Authenticating documents before relying on them, as AI makes forged evidence cheap
problem: Regulators warn that AI tools can create realistic false evidence, so a clean-looking invoice or vendor file no longer signals legitimacy.
approach: MindBridge advises matching invoice details to bank records and system metadata; a BDO practitioner advises scanning vendor masters for suspicious entries.
Whether firms use automated authenticity-detection tools in substantive testing was not found.
The auditor decides whether evidence is authentic enough to rely on, with out-of-band verification of suspicious items.

title: Idea: testing AI-generated client information, or the controls over it
problem: This is an idea, not a deployment: when a client uses AI to categorise expenses or prepare accruals, the auditor may not see how the output was produced.
approach: The AICPA practice aid (October 2026) says auditors may test AI outputs substantively; if that is not enough, they should test controls.
Where the process is a black box, the auditor may need to relate inputs to outputs and explore non-traditional evidence sources.
The auditor decides whether substantive tests alone suffice or controls must be tested.

title: Generative AI assistant helps teams design substantive procedures (KPMG Clara)
problem: Teams must tailor substantive procedures to assessed risks and the entity, which means reading engagement documents and methodology.
approach: KPMG said in July 2024 it had integrated generative AI into Clara for 90,000 auditors to develop substantive procedures.
The assistant works with engagement documentation and methodology. No outcomes published (self-reported).
The engagement team member stays responsible for results and documentation, and auditors remain in control of decisions.

title: Excel agent cleans and reconciles ledger data to the trial balance
problem: Raw client data arrives with mixed fields, inconsistent dates and blank rows, and preparing it for testing is repetitive, slow and error-prone.
approach: Two University of Akron academics built a ChatGPT Excel agent that asks approval before changing data and reconciles to the trial balance.
A simulated clean, validate and reconcile of 59,157 rows took about 10 minutes, against many hours manually (independent, per the authors).
The auditor approves the plan and reviews the reconciliation and the generated documentation.

title: Technology-assisted selection of items to test
problem: PCAOB standards covered audit samples but not items chosen when testing all items or specific items, and auditors were already using technology to choose them.
approach: Tools identify and select journal entries, high-risk items or samples; amended PCAOB rules apply the same testing requirements however items are selected.
All six US network firms reported tools that select samples (self-reported); a Thomson Reuters customer says they significantly improve sample selection (vendor-published).
The auditor challenges how the tool classified items as low risk and decides what testing the unflagged remainder needs.
who: US global network firms, Thomson Reuters, Oberlander

title: AI risk scoring to cut substantive sample sizes (Cherry Bekaert on MindBridge)
problem: Firms relying only on a third-party audit methodology may need much of their assurance from sampling, tying up seniors for hours selecting or testing items.
approach: Cherry Bekaert adopted MindBridge in 2020 and built it deliberately: standards mapping, methodology, quality-control validation and firm-wide policy.
The aim is more assurance from risk scoring of full populations, hence smaller samples; 66% reduction on an illustrative client (vendor-published).
Associates keep autonomy to make decisions and exercise professional judgment.

title: Agents match sampled items to supporting documents and bank activity
problem: Vouching means opening many differently formatted invoices, contracts and bank records and tracing each sampled amount by hand; one customer put it at about two full days per engagement.
approach: Tools extract data from varied documents, match sampled items to evidence and flag gaps. Users include PwC, Thomson Reuters, Sanville & Co.
A Kentucky firm owner reports engagement time falling from about two days to five or six hours (vendor-published).
Auditors work the exceptions and analyse differences; each match carries an evidence trail a reviewer can check.
who: PwC, Thomson Reuters, Sanville & Co, Fieldguide

title: Firm-built Excel agents for evidence-heavy tests of details (FGMK on DataSnipper)
problem: FGMK auditors often receive unorganised client files, such as PDFs of over 100 pages, so preparers and reviewers spend significant time finding evidence for each selection.
approach: A pilot group at FGMK used DataSnipper Excel Agents to find evidence in client PDFs and trace revenue to contracts.
Time per selection fell from 30-45 minutes to about 5 minutes of review (vendor-published); firm-wide adoption is planned.
Reviewer-side agents check consistency across a workbook. The auditor signs off at the end.

title: Excel evidence snipping and AI extraction for tie-out and vouching (DataSnipper)
problem: Auditors reconcile numbers from invoices, bank statements and inventory documents to transactions by hand, and reviewers must re-find the evidence.
approach: The auditor snips values from source documents into Excel, keeping a link to the source; AI adds extraction from unstructured documents.
DataSnipper says AI pre-validated more than two million data points from client documents in 2025 (vendor-published).
The auditor selects and snips the evidence; the reviewer clicks through to the source.

title: Automated financial-statement tie-out and testing in fund audits (PwC pilot)
problem: Fund audits require financial-statement tie-outs and testing of extracted data and documents, a large volume of repeat work per engagement.
approach: PwC's tool extracts, organises and tests financial data and documents for non-registered fund-to-fund audits, automating parts of tie-out and testing.
In October 2025 it was being tested with certain asset and wealth management engagement teams, with a plan to expand the pilot.
No outcomes published (self-reported); human checkpoints are not described in the source.

title: Language-model contract and lease review to target revenue and lease testing
problem: Checking many contracts or contracts spanning hundreds of pages is repetitive and slow, and a tool that only screens for a term can be mistaken for a complete read.
approach: Thomson Reuters' CoCounsel Document Analysis uses agentic AI to review client documents at scale; early adopters report up to 70% faster (vendor-published).
The UK regulator's illustrative design extracts risk indicators from contracts and scores each one; those above a threshold form the sample.
The auditor sees which indicators were present, tests the selected contracts, and cannot assume checking is done once AI has helped.

title: Agents applied to judgment-heavy tests such as complex revenue and memo checks
problem: Revenue with complex terms such as rebates needs judgment-heavy testing that routine tools did not cover, and memos can describe something the data does not support.
approach: PwC's US assurance transformation leader said the firm was applying AI agents to assess whether US pharmaceutical rebate revenue was recorded properly.
EY's assurance AI leader expects agents to flag memos not supported by the data; this is an expectation, not a result.
No outcomes published (self-reported). Humans oversee agent testing and the auditor reviews flagged inconsistencies.

title: Analytical procedures with technology-built expectations from detailed or unstructured data
problem: Year-over-year comparisons dominate substantive analytics; only 11% of 54 surveyed US firms have an automated solution, and practice has diverged on how such procedures are categorised.
approach: Draft ISA 520 guidance says tools may structure unstructured industry reports or model revenue against cost of sales to sharpen expectations.
Deloitte Netherlands (internal audit) and KPMG (SOX) describe 100% transaction coverage where data quality allows.
The auditor judges whether the expectation is precise enough, investigates differences and obtains evidence for management's explanations.

title: Digital confirmation platforms and direct, authenticated access to bank data
problem: Firms prepared and chased bank, customer and supplier confirmations by hand, and external evidence often arrives as screenshots or PDFs that can be forged cheaply.
approach: Platforms create, send and track confirmations and authenticate responses. Users include Moore Polska and Crowe Spain; BDO NL tested direct bank feeds.
The vendor's case study says Moore Polska saved up to 20 hours per audit (vendor-published).
The auditor controls the confirmation request, judges response reliability and investigates anomalies that bank-data analytics flag.
who: Moore Polska, Crowe Spain, BDO NL, Circit

title: Drone and imaging tools for inventory counts
problem: Inventory observation requires auditors at counts of large warehouses and outdoor stock, which is slow and disruptive; standards are unclear on remote observation.
approach: EY ran a 2018 proof of concept where drones scan barcodes and labels and send data to the audit platform for reconciliation.
An academic study found drone counts took 19 hours against 681 manually, with error rates falling from 0.15% to 0.03% (independent).
The auditor sets scan parameters and sampling, reconciles results and judges the evidence obtained by alternative means.

title: Idea: AI-generated independent expectations and challenge for accounting estimates
problem: This is an idea, not a deployment: accounting estimates had the highest finding rate in IFIAR's 2025 survey, 112 of 498 inspected audits (22%).
approach: An AI system supplies contradictory evidence or an alternative estimate that the auditor weighs against management's estimate.
In an experiment, auditors given contradictory evidence by their firm's AI proposed smaller adjustments than those given it by a human specialist.
The auditor evaluates the evidence, any specialist's advice and management's estimate, and decides on adjustments.

title: Agents run routine substantive tests, moving to orchestrated end-to-end runs
problem: Routine testing such as expense vouching and unrecorded-liability searches means pulling samples, extracting data and marking pass or fail, which absorbs junior staff time.
approach: KPMG announced Clara agents (April 2025) for expense vouching and unrecorded liabilities; in April 2026 it described orchestration agents, piloting summer 2026.
Fieldguide says its Field Orchestrator went live in June 2026, with the unrecorded-liabilities search as its first end-to-end test.
The auditor confirms the plan, reviews outputs after each phase and exceptions, and signs off. No measured results (self-reported).

title: Auditor and client agents exchange evidence requests, with workpapers reviewed (EY pilot)
problem: Selecting items, requesting and chasing client support, and assembling workpapers is manual and slow.
approach: EY described pilots where its agents make preliminary selections and request support; the client's agents collect and send it back.
EY's agents then prepare workpapers. EY says its multi-agent framework is embedded in all audit phases, with end-to-end support expected by 2028.
Humans review the workpapers the agents prepare. No outcomes published (self-reported).

title: Firm-wide agent platforms draft substantive workpapers for review (EY, Deloitte, Grant Thornton)
problem: Global firms need consistent methodology across thousands of engagements, and staff fieldwork takes hours per workpaper; a benchmark team estimated 2-12 hours each.
approach: Deloitte (June 2026) says Omnia agents execute preliminary procedures; EY (April 2026) and Grant Thornton US (May 2026) describe similar agent platforms.
In a benchmark, the best model strictly passed 69.17% of workpaper tasks in one attempt but 44.44% across all eight attempts (vendor-published).
Professionals review preliminary conclusions, and Grant Thornton says professionals supervise every step.

title: Idea: a second AI reviews AI-performed substantive work for errors
problem: This is an idea, not a deployment: senior review of staff workpapers takes time and can miss errors, and AI tools could review work for omissions or inconsistencies.
approach: The AICPA practice aid says one AI tool may perform a procedure and another review it, without reducing the auditor's supervision duties.
In a benchmark, the best reviewing model raised strict pass on agent-completed workpapers from 28.89% to 62.22% (vendor-published).
A human reviewer remains responsible for the reviewed workpaper.

title: AI-native audit pilot testing full populations instead of samples (PwC Australia)
problem: Auditors spend time on data gathering and documentation rather than analysis, and sampling limits the scrutiny applied to balances.
approach: PwC Australia said in October 2025 it was rolling out an AI-native platform in a global pilot, with agents testing full populations.
It starts with five audit clients and plans to reach all by 2028. No results published (self-reported).
The auditor investigates every item identified and the team reviews whether the tool met its objective; PwC says humans keep final judgments.

title: Specialist audit firm built to test every transaction in benefit-plan audits (Ledgerline)
problem: The annual 401(k) audit is described as a four-month chore of requests and follow-ups, with testing a sample of contributions extrapolated to the plan.
approach: Ledgerline, a pre-launch specialist audit firm, says it will pull data from source systems and test the whole population, not a sample.
Its CEO says AI agents paired with deterministic code can check every deposit and distribution and cite the plan provision tested.
A person stays accountable for every conclusion. No outcomes published (self-reported).
